objectives: I can plot Boolean functions on 2-, 3- and 4-variable Karnaugh maps using Gray-code ordering.
I can group 1s legally (powers of two, as large as possible, overlapping and wrapping allowed) and read off the minimised expression.
I can state the logic of a half adder and a full adder and explain how full adders chain to add multi-bit numbers.
I can describe how a D-type flip-flop stores one bit on a clock edge and how flip-flops form a register.

retrieval.a: ¬A ∧ ¬B: break the bar, swap ∨ for ∧, negate each term.

retrieval.q: From 1.4.3 part 1: simplify A ∨ (A ∧ B) and name the law.
From 1.4.3 part 1: what does A ⊻ B output when A = 1 and B = 1?
retrieval.a: 0: XOR outputs 1 only when the inputs differ.

retrieval.q: From 1.4.3 part 1: how many rows does a truth table for a 3-input expression need, and in what order?
retrieval.a: 2 to the power 3 = 8 rows, counted in binary from 000 to 111.

retrieval.a: De Morgan's gives ¬(¬A) ∧ ¬B; double negation gives A ∧ ¬B.

keywords.def: A grid of truth-table outputs arranged so adjacent cells differ in exactly one variable, used to minimise expressions.
An ordering of binary values (00, 01, 11, 10) where consecutive values differ in exactly one bit.
A rectangle of 1s on a K-map containing 1, 2, 4 or 8 cells, as large as possible, which may overlap or wrap.
An expression ORing together AND terms, e.g. (¬B ∧ ¬D) ∨ (B ∧ D); the form a K-map reads off.
A circuit adding two bits: Sum = A ⊻ B, Carry = A ∧ B; it has no carry-in.
A circuit adding three bits (A, B, Cin), built from two half adders and an OR gate, giving Sum and Cout.
Full adders chained so each carry-out feeds the next column's carry-in, adding multi-bit numbers.
An edge-triggered circuit that stores the value of its D input at the clock edge and holds it at output Q.
Circuits whose output depends on stored state as well as current inputs, unlike combinational gates and adders.

content.heading: Why minimise a circuit?
points: Every operator in an expression is a physical gate: fewer operators means fewer gates.
Fewer gates means cheaper, faster and lower-power circuits.
Boolean laws minimise algebraically; a Karnaugh map does the same job visually.
K-maps make the simplification hard to get wrong: the groups do the algebra for you.

content.heading: K-map layout and Gray code
points: A K-map is the truth table redrawn as a grid, one cell per input row.
Row and column headings use Gray-code order: 00, 01, 11, 10, not binary order.
Gray code means neighbouring cells differ in exactly one variable.
That adjacency is the whole trick: neighbouring 1s can merge, eliminating the variable that differs.
content.note: Writing columns 00, 01, 10, 11 in binary order breaks adjacency and wrecks every grouping.

content.heading: Two-variable K-maps
points: A 2x2 grid: rows A = 0, 1; columns B = 0, 1; four cells for four truth-table rows.
Copy each output into its cell, then circle groups of 1s.
Example: 1s in both cells where B = 1, across both rows, group as a vertical pair.
Inside the group A changes but B stays 1, so the expression is just B.

content.heading: Three-variable K-maps
points: A 2x4 grid: rows A = 0, 1; columns BC in Gray order 00, 01, 11, 10.
Top row holds rows 000, 001, 011, 010 of the truth table; note 011 before 010.
Bottom row holds 100, 101, 111, 110.
The left and right columns (BC = 00 and BC = 10) are adjacent: the map wraps around.

content.heading: The grouping rules
points: Circle 1s only, in rectangles of 1, 2, 4 or 8 cells: powers of two only, never 3 or 6.
Make every group as large as legally possible, even if groups overlap.
Groups may wrap across the map's edges; on a 4-variable map the four corners form one group.
Every 1 must be inside at least one group; each group becomes one AND term.

content.heading: Reading off the minimised expression
points: Interrogate each group: which variables have the same value in every cell inside it?
Variables that stay constant survive: value 1 keeps the variable, value 0 keeps its negation.
Variables that change inside the group are eliminated.
OR the groups' terms together for the final sum-of-products expression.
Each doubling of group size eliminates one variable: bigger groups mean simpler terms.

content.heading: Four-variable K-maps
points: A 4x4 grid: rows AB and columns CD, both in Gray order 00, 01, 11, 10.
Sixteen cells cover the sixteen rows of a 4-input truth table.
Wrapping works both ways: top row is adjacent to bottom row, left column to right column.
The four corner cells are mutually adjacent and can form a single group of 4.
content.note: Groups of 8 eliminate three variables, leaving a single-letter term.

content.heading: The half adder
points: Adds two single bits A and B, producing a Sum bit and a Carry bit.
Sum = A ⊻ B and Carry = A ∧ B: one XOR gate and one AND gate.
Truth table: 0+0 gives Sum 0 Carry 0; 0+1 and 1+0 give Sum 1 Carry 0; 1+1 gives Sum 0 Carry 1.
1 + 1 = binary 10: the Carry is the twos column, which is why Carry = A ∧ B.
content.note: The half adder has no carry-in, so it can only be the rightmost column of an addition.

content.heading: The full adder
points: Adds three bits: A, B and a carry-in Cin from the previous column.
Built from two half adders plus an OR gate combining their two carry outputs.
Sum = A ⊻ B ⊻ Cin and Cout = (A ∧ B) ∨ (Cin ∧ (A ⊻ B)).
Chaining full adders, each Cout feeding the next Cin, makes a ripple-carry adder for whole binary numbers.

content.heading: The D-type flip-flop
points: A 1-bit memory: output Q takes the value of input D only at the active clock edge.
Between clock edges Q holds its stored value, however much D changes.
The clock is a regular pulse; edge-triggering synchronises when data is captured.
This is sequential logic: output depends on stored state, unlike combinational gates and adders.
Uses: one flip-flop per bit in registers, counters and memory; eight side by side store a byte.

worked_examples.title: Three-variable K-map: F(A,B,C) is 1 on rows 000, 001, 100, 101
steps: Draw the 2x4 map: rows A = 0, 1; columns BC in Gray order 00, 01, 11, 10.
Plot the 1s: row A=0 gets 1s under columns 00 and 01; row A=1 gets 1s under columns 00 and 01.
The four 1s form one 2x2 square on the left: a single legal group of 4.
Interrogate the group: A is 0 and 1 inside (eliminated); C is 0 and 1 inside (eliminated); B is 0 in every cell.
B constant at 0 survives as its negation, so F = ¬B.
Verify: the four rows 000, 001, 100, 101 are exactly the rows with B = 0, so F = ¬B is correct.

worked_examples.title: Four-variable K-map with wrap-around: F(A,B,C,D) is 1 on rows 0000, 0010, 0101, 0111, 1000, 1010, 1101, 1111
steps: Draw the 4x4 map: rows AB and columns CD, both in Gray order 00, 01, 11, 10.
Plot cell by cell: row AB=00 gets 1s in columns CD=00 (row 0000) and CD=10 (row 0010).
Row AB=01 gets 1s in columns CD=01 (0101) and CD=11 (0111); row AB=11 gets 1s in CD=01 (1101) and CD=11 (1111).
Row AB=10 gets 1s in columns CD=00 (1000) and CD=10 (1010). Eight 1s plotted, eight cells left as 0.
Group 1: the four corners (0000, 0010, 1000, 1010) are adjacent by wrapping both ways: one group of 4.
Interrogate the corners: A varies, C varies; B = 0 and D = 0 in all four cells, giving ¬B ∧ ¬D.
Group 2: the centre 2x2 square (0101, 0111, 1101, 1111): A varies, C varies; B = 1 and D = 1 throughout, giving B ∧ D.
F = (¬B ∧ ¬D) ∨ (B ∧ D). Check: the eight 1-cells are exactly the rows where B and D are equal, and every 0-cell has B and D different, so the expression matches all sixteen cells.

worked_examples.title: Building a full adder from two half adders and tracing 1 + 1 + 1
steps: Half adder 1 takes A and B: S1 = A ⊻ B and C1 = A ∧ B.
Half adder 2 takes S1 and Cin: Sum = S1 ⊻ Cin = A ⊻ B ⊻ Cin, and C2 = S1 ∧ Cin.
An OR gate combines the carries: Cout = C1 ∨ C2 = (A ∧ B) ∨ (Cin ∧ (A ⊻ B)).
Trace A = 1, B = 1, Cin = 1: half adder 1 gives S1 = 1 ⊻ 1 = 0 and C1 = 1 ∧ 1 = 1.
Half adder 2 gives Sum = 0 ⊻ 1 = 1 and C2 = 0 ∧ 1 = 0.
Cout = 1 ∨ 0 = 1, so the outputs are Sum = 1, Cout = 1: binary 11, which is 3, correct for 1 + 1 + 1.
Full truth table check (A B Cin, Sum, Cout): 000 gives 0,0; 001, 010 and 100 give 1,0; 011, 101 and 110 give 0,1; 111 gives 1,1.

activities.title: K-Map Twister (floor-sized Karnaugh map)
instructions: Tape a 2x4 K-map on the floor: rows A = 0, 1; columns BC in Gray order 00, 01, 11, 10; make the class explain why 11 comes before 10 (adjacent cells must differ by one bit).
Read out a truth table for F(A,B,C) that is 1 on rows 000, 001, 100, 101; one student stands in each 1-cell.
The class lassos the standing students with string: loops only in powers of two, as large as possible, rectangles only, wrapping allowed.
The loopers interrogate the enclosed cells: which variable is the same for everyone inside? Answer: B = 0 everywhere, so F = ¬B; A and C change, so they are eliminated.
Repeat with F = 1 on rows 000, 010, 100, 110: columns 00 and 10 are adjacent only by wrapping, one wrapped group of 4 where C = 0 throughout, so F = ¬C.
activities.stretch: Add row 111 to the first function as a lone student: the class must find the best legal grouping (pair 111 with 101 to get A ∧ C, giving F = ¬B ∨ (A ∧ C)).

activities.title: The Human Half Adder, then Full Adder (circuit walk)
instructions: Inputs A and B stand at one wall; one XOR student and one AND student are both fed by A and B; label XOR's output Sum and AND's output Carry.
Walk all four input combinations, recording the truth table on the board: 00 gives Sum 0 Carry 0; 01 and 10 give Sum 1 Carry 0; 11 gives Sum 0 Carry 1.
Ask: what operation have we built out of people? (Binary addition of two bits: 1 + 1 = 10.)
Bolt on a third input Cin, a second half adder taking Sum and Cin, and an OR student combining the two carries: a full adder.
Verify the hardest row together: A = 1, B = 1, Cin = 1 gives Sum = 1 and Cout = 1 (binary 11 = 3).
activities.stretch: Line up three full-adder teams as a ripple-carry adder and add 011 + 011, watching the carry ripple left (answer 110 = 6).

activities.title: The Human D-Type Flip-Flop
instructions: One student is the D input: they may change their 0/1 card whenever they like and are encouraged to fidget. A second student is the flip-flop holding the Q card: they may only look at D and copy it at the exact moment the teacher claps (the rising clock edge). Between claps they freeze.
Run the script with the class predicting Q before each event: start Q = 0; D shows 1, clap; D changes to 0 with no clap; wait, then clap; D flickers 1, 0, 1 rapidly with no clap; clap.
Expected trace: clap 1 makes Q = 1; Q stays 1 while D drops (the class should protest if the flip-flop flinches); clap 2 makes Q = 0; Q stays 0 through the flicker; clap 3 makes Q = 1.
Ask: what is this student doing, in one word? (Remembering: it is 1-bit memory.)
Add three more flip-flop students sharing the same clap: a 4-bit register storing a nibble on one synchronised edge.
activities.stretch: Chain two flip-flops (Q of the first feeds D of the second) and clap twice: the bit marches one stage per clock pulse, a shift register.

practice.q: State the Boolean expressions for the Sum and Carry outputs of a half adder. [2]
practice.a: Sum = A ⊻ B (1); Carry = A ∧ B (1).

practice.q: Explain why full adders, not half adders, are needed to add two 8-bit binary numbers. [2]
practice.a: Every column after the least significant may receive a carry from the column to its right, so it must add three bits (1); a half adder has no carry-in, but full adders chain carry-out to carry-in as a ripple-carry adder (1).

practice.q: A 2-variable Karnaugh map has 1s in both cells where B = 1, for A = 0 and A = 1. Write the minimised expression. [1]
practice.a: F = B: inside the group of 2, A changes (eliminated) and B stays at 1.

practice.q: F(A,B,C) is 1 on rows 000, 010, 100 and 110. Explain how a Karnaugh map groups these cells and state the minimised expression. [3]
practice.a: The 1s fill columns BC = 00 and BC = 10 in both rows; these columns are adjacent by wrap-around (1), so all four cells form one group of 4 (1). A and B vary inside but C = 0 throughout, so F = ¬C (1).

practice.q: Complete the full adder outputs for the row A = 1, B = 0, Cin = 1. [2]
Describe what happens to the Q output of a D-type flip-flop when D changes between clock edges. [2]
practice.a: Nothing: Q holds the value stored at the last active clock edge (1); Q only updates to the current value of D at the next active edge (1).

practice.q: Explain how D-type flip-flops can be used to build a 4-bit register. [2]
practice.a: One flip-flop stores each bit, so four are placed side by side (1); they share the same clock signal, so all four bits are captured on the same edge, storing the value in a synchronised way (1).

practice.q: State two rules for grouping 1s on a Karnaugh map and explain why larger groups are preferred. [3]
practice.a: Groups must be rectangles containing a power of two cells: 1, 2, 4 or 8 (1); groups may overlap and may wrap around the map's edges (1). Each doubling of group size eliminates one variable, so larger groups give simpler terms and fewer gates (1).

misconceptions: Students often label K-map columns in binary order 00, 01, 10, 11; the order must be Gray code 00, 01, 11, 10 so adjacent cells differ in one variable.
Students often circle groups of 3 or 6; groups must be powers of two (1, 2, 4, 8) and rectangular.
Students often forget that K-maps wrap: the left and right edges are adjacent, the top and bottom edges are adjacent, and the four corners can form one group.
Students often give a half adder a carry-in; it adds only two bits, which is exactly why the full adder exists.
Students often think a flip-flop's output follows D continuously; Q changes only at the active clock edge, which is what makes it memory rather than a wire.
exam_link: Command words seen here: complete for K-maps and adder truth tables (2-4 marks), write or state for minimised expressions (1-2 marks), describe and explain for adders and flip-flops (2-4 marks).
K-map questions usually give the completed map and ask for legal groupings plus the minimised expression; illegal group sizes score zero for that group.
Sum = A ⊻ B and Carry = A ∧ B must be quoted exactly; describing the full adder as two half adders plus an OR gate is a standard 3-mark build.
Example stem: 'The Karnaugh map for a logic circuit is shown. Draw the groups and write the simplified Boolean expression for the circuit.' [4]
task: Draw the 2x4 Karnaugh map for F(A,B,C) which is 1 on rows 000, 001, 100, 101 and 111. Group the 1s legally and write the minimised expression. (Answer: the left 2x2 square gives ¬B; row 111 pairs with 101, where A = 1 and C = 1 throughout, giving A ∧ C; so F = ¬B ∨ (A ∧ C). Check row 111: ¬B = 0 but A ∧ C = 1, so F = 1 as required.)
challenge: Three full adders are chained as a ripple-carry adder. Trace the addition 011 + 011 column by column, giving Sum and Cout for each adder, and state the final answer. (Column 0: 1+1+0 gives Sum 0, carry 1. Column 1: 1+1+1 gives Sum 1, carry 1. Column 2: 0+0+1 gives Sum 1, carry 0. Result 110 = 6, which is 3 + 3. Explain why the carry is called a ripple.)

exit_ticket.q: Why are K-map columns ordered 00, 01, 11, 10 rather than in binary order?
exit_ticket.a: Gray-code order makes adjacent cells differ in exactly one variable, so neighbouring 1s can group and eliminate that variable.

exit_ticket.q: What are the half adder's outputs when A = 1 and B = 1?
exit_ticket.a: Sum = 0 and Carry = 1 (binary 10), since Sum = A ⊻ B and Carry = A ∧ B.

exit_ticket.q: When does a D-type flip-flop change its Q output, and to what value?
exit_ticket.a: Only at the active clock edge, when Q takes the current value of the D input; between edges it holds its stored bit.
